 Six in Ten New Yorkers Back a $30 Minimum Wage
 New findings from the 2026 Cornell ILR Empire State Poll
 by Russell Weaver 
 New York State’s minimum wage is about to stop increasing. A weak summer jobs report triggered an “off-ramp” in state law, so the $16 and $17 hourly rates will not rise on January 1, 2027, even though prices in the New York area climbed 4.5% over the past year. The federal minimum, meanwhile, has sat at $7.25 since 2009.
 New Yorkers want something very different. In the 2026 Cornell ILR-CAROW Empire State Poll, released for the first time in a new data brief, 60% of New York adults say the state should raise its minimum wage to at least $30 an hour , about what MIT estimates a single adult needs to cover basic costs here. In New York City, support reaches 75%.
 What the poll found
 Source: Cornell ILR-CAROW Empire State Poll 2026, Q31, weighted, 2,628 respondents. Margins of error and sample sizes are in the full brief.
 A statewide majority. 60% of New Yorkers say yes and 40% say no (margin of error ±2.6 points). 
 New York City leads. Support is 75% in the city and 49% in the rest of the state. The Bronx is highest at 88%, followed by Manhattan (75%), Brooklyn (74%), and Queens (69%). 
 The City’s lead goes beyond who lives there. City residents are more supportive than their counterparts elsewhere in every group we examined, including Republicans (59% vs. 30%) and homeowners (62% vs. 36%). Even after accounting for age, gender, race, education, income, housing, and party, living in NYC adds about 9 points. 
 Individuals closest to the wage floor want it raised the most. About eight in ten young adults, renters, and New Yorkers with family incomes under $30,000 say yes, as do 89% of Black New Yorkers, 81% of Hispanic or Latina/o New Yorkers, and 71% of hourly workers. 
 Support held as the bar rose. In 2024, 62.4% of New Yorkers backed a $26 minimum. Today, 60% back $30. 
 Why it matters
 The $30 figure in the poll is not arbitrary. MIT’s Living Wage Calculator puts the living wage for a single adult in New York at $29.89 an hour. A full-time job at $17 covers less than half of a single adult’s living wage in Manhattan and under 60% in the Bronx. And with the 2027 raise on hold, New York City’s $17 minimum now buys 14% less than its $15 minimum did in January 2019. 
 The findings also land in the middle of New York City’s own push for $30. Mayor Zohran Mamdani campaigned on “$30 by ’30,” and the Raise Up NY coalition is backing Int. 0757, the $30 for Our City Act, in the City Council. Under current law, though, only Albany sets the minimum wage, so the city would first need the Legislature to pass a bill like S3952 letting it set its own. Governor Hochul, for her part, has asked lawmakers to restore a smaller raise in March 2027 when they return in January. 
 Three in four city residents already back a $30 minimum statewide. That is a strong public mandate for both fights. 
 Our new data brief, Raising the Floor: New York’s Minimum Wage and the Case for a Living Wage , breaks down this data in several additional ways: 
 Results for every age, income, race and ethnicity, party, borough, and region, with margins of error 
 How far the NYS and federal minimum wages have fallen behind prices and living costs; 
 A guide to the active proposals in Albany, City Hall and Congress; and 
 Seven implications for lawmakers, from repealing the off-ramp to letting New York City set its own floor. 
 Read the Brief 
 The 2026 Cornell ILR-CAROW Empire State Poll surveyed 2,629 New York adults online from June 24 to July 8, 2026. Results are weighted, and the margin of error for the full sample is ±2.6 points. 
 Russell Weaver
 Economic Geographer, ILR Buffalo Co-Lab
